summary: Armenia is visa-free for a broad range of passports — the EU, UK, US, Russia, Japan, the Gulf states and several other CIS and Latin American countries can stay up to 180 days per year, and China up to 90 days — while most other nationalities can obtain an e-Visa online or a visa on arrival at Zvartnots Airport. A smaller group of nationalities must apply through an embassy with an invitation.

defaultStayWindow.text: The MFA states that citizens of countries with a visa-free regime “can stay on the territory of the Republic of Armenia for no more than 180 days during one year if no other term is defined by the international agreements”, and elsewhere on the same page puts the same allowance as 180 days “within any one-year period”. It is a rolling twelve months rather than a calendar year. The MFA does not say whether the days of arrival and departure are counted, so we count both.

safety.text: Armenia is generally safe with low crime, and Yerevan is comfortable to walk even late in the evening. Avoid the immediate border areas with Azerbaijan, where the situation can change quickly. Check current advice before visiting frontier regions.

bestTimeToVisit.text: Late spring and early fall are ideal — warm days for monasteries and hiking without the intense summer heat of the Ararat plain; winter is cold but good for skiing at Tsaghkadzor.

idp.text: Armenia is a party to the 1968 Vienna Convention on Road Traffic but not to the 1949 Geneva one, so the International Driving Permit it is bound to recognize is the 1968 Vienna version. A permit issued under the 1949 Geneva Convention carries no treaty obligation here.

tips.text: Armenia's land borders with Turkey and Azerbaijan are closed — overland you can only enter from Georgia or Iran, otherwise fly into Yerevan.
Stay clear of the immediate frontier with Azerbaijan, including some road sections that run close to the border. The security situation there can change quickly.
Yerevan's public drinking fountains (pulpulaks) are safe and everywhere — tap water throughout Armenia is generally excellent.
Use the GG or Yandex Go apps for taxis, or agree the fare before setting off — street taxis rarely run their meters for visitors.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Armenia?
faq.answer: Probably not. Citizens of the EU, UK, US, Russia, Japan, the Gulf states and several other CIS and Latin American countries enter visa-free and can stay up to 180 days per year; Chinese citizens can stay up to 90 days in any 180. Most other nationalities can apply online for an e-Visa (21 or 120 days) or obtain a visa on arrival at Zvartnots Airport; some nationalities need an invitation and must apply through an embassy.

faq.question: How long can I stay in Armenia visa-free?
faq.answer: Visa-waiver nationalities may stay up to 180 days per calendar year in total. Longer stays require a residence permit from the migration authorities.

faq.question: Can I get an Armenian visa on arrival?
faq.answer: Yes — e-Visa-eligible nationalities can obtain a visitor visa on arrival at Zvartnots Airport and at open land crossings: AMD 3,000 for 21 days or AMD 15,000 for 120 days. Applying online in advance at evisa.mfa.am avoids any line.

faq.question: Can I visit Armenia after Azerbaijan, or with Azerbaijani stamps in my passport?
faq.answer: Yes — Armenia does not refuse entry over Azerbaijani visas or stamps, though officers may ask about your trip. The reverse is different: Azerbaijan refuses entry to travelers with evidence of visits to Nagorno-Karabakh.

faq.question: Is the land border between Armenia and Turkey open?
faq.answer: No. It has been closed since the 1990s, as has the border with Azerbaijan. To combine Armenia and Turkey in one trip, fly (Yerevan–Istanbul flights operate) or route overland through Georgia.
